source_user: Advanced cluster case cluster scheduling and recovery-48: Design a resilient cluster scheduler for distributed LLM training and inference. Variant 48 must state assumptions, define a falsifiable hypothesis, name metrics, and include one failure or rollback condition.
source_assistant: An expert answer should distinguish model-domain mechanisms from runtime measurements. Required technical anchors: cover gang scheduling, GPU/NIC/topology-aware placement, fragmentation, preemption, checkpoint cadence, node drain, elastic restart, replica routing, SLOs, and resource accounting. It must report topology, workload, units, baselines, confounders, and evidence needed before claiming improvement.
corrected_answer:
For variant 48, treat resilience as a measured scheduler-and-recovery property, not an assumed platform feature. Assumptions: jobs declare GPU type/count, CPU, memory, storage, NIC/RDMA, NUMA and GPU topology, parallelism shape, priority, checkpoint format/interval, and inference SLOs; inventory, admission, placement, preemption, fencing, routing, and failure events are observable. Platform semantics and capacity remain hypotheses until measured.

Falsifiable hypothesis: topology-aware gang admission, fragmentation-aware packing, checkpoint-aware preemption, and bounded node-drain recovery reduce wasted GPU-hours and p95 recovery time without violating inference availability or latency SLOs versus the current policy. Hold workload mix, model, inventory, checkpoint policy, and routing policy fixed in matched baseline and canary windows.

Design: admit distributed training jobs atomically only when GPU/NIC/NUMA constraints fit; expose queue reasons and fragmentation rather than partially starting a gang. Reserve topology-compatible capacity and account CPU, memory, storage, GPU-hours, and network capacity. Preempt only at safe checkpoint boundaries, record checkpoint age and integrity, fence failed or draining nodes before restart, and use elastic restart with bounded retries and idempotent recovery. Route inference replicas using health, capacity, topology, and load signals; shed or queue work rather than silently violating SLOs. Use priorities and quotas with fairness limits so training cannot starve serving.

Measure scheduler queue and admission latency (s), placement/fragmentation rate (%), utilization (%), preemption and checkpoint overhead (s and GPU-hours), restart success rate (%), checkpoint recovery point/objective gaps, node-drain and failure recovery p50/p95 (s), inference availability (%), request p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), throughput (requests/s or tokens/s), error rate (%), and resource accounting reconciliation (GPU-hours, CPU-hours, GiB-hours, network bytes). Compare matched workloads with synchronized timestamps, topology/inventory snapshots, confidence intervals, and failure-mode stratification; distinguish measured facts from estimates and test confounders such as thermal throttling, network contention, autoscaling, model-cache state, and failure injection realism.

Rollback or failure conditions: halt canary and restore the prior scheduling/routing policy if availability or latency breaches its SLO budget, recovery p95 regresses beyond a pre-registered margin, checkpoint integrity fails, fencing is not confirmed, resource accounting diverges, or unauthorized cross-tenant placement is observed. Use least-privilege diagnostics, redact tenant and credential data, preserve audit logs, and obtain topology, matched traces, checkpoint-integrity/recovery results, failure-injection results, and independent domain review before operational claims. Results are provisional, not expert gold.
risks: Platform-specific topology, fencing, elastic restart, and routing semantics may differ from assumptions.
Synthetic scenario lacks measured workload, failure traces, and independent review.

Matched baseline/canary traces with synchronized timestamps and units
